Back to Sound Elevator

Heights, sounds & field notes

66 discoveries from across Earth, arranged in five equally long height chapters.

What each height means

Each answer explains its height connection: a measured body or structure, a nest or flight range, a vertical experiment, an elevation above sea level, or an atmospheric calculation. Natural ranges remain ranges. The sources below identify the measurement and its reference level. Illustrations are stylised, not scale drawings or documentary photographs.

The five bands contain 13, 11, 12, 16 and 14 stops. Each chapter has the same scroll length, with evenly spaced stops inside it. Between anchors, the counter uses logarithmic height interpolation. The first soil scene remains at ground level.

The atmosphere readouts

These are model values for geometric altitude above sea level—not live weather, cabin conditions, or the ambient conditions at a pictured object whose datum is relative to its base. The lower atmosphere uses the ISA-compatible seven-layer hydrostatic equations of the U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976, including geometric-to-geopotential conversion. From 86–100 km, temperature uses the COESA upper-atmosphere equations and pressure/density use logarithmic interpolation of Table I, page 68. The tiny 80–86 km molecular-weight temperature correction is interpolated approximately (less than 0.1°C).

Pressure is expressed as a percentage of 101,325 Pa. IAPWS saturation pressure gives water’s boiling temperature; below 611.657 Pa, stable liquid water is unavailable and the readout says “No liquid.” This is an equilibrium model, not a claim that an exposed drop disappears instantly.

Sound speed is the ideal dry-gas value √(1.4p/ρ). In extremely thin upper air this is a theoretical local gas property, not a promise that human speech remains audible. Temperature can depart greatly from the model: polar summer mesopause air, for example, can be much colder.

Horizon distance is √(2Rh + h²), with Earth radius 6,371 km. It ignores terrain and refraction and measures the straight sightline to the geometric horizon; at ordinary heights it closely matches 3.57√h km. Gravity at 100 km is calculated from the inverse-square law, yielding 96.93% of the spherical surface value.

Below the surface

Negative heights are depths below local ground, not elevations below sea level. This route brings together different locations. Scenes marked illustrative are not measurements or a claim that these features occupy the same vertical shaft. The cave and train recordings are genuine field recordings; rain in the shallow soil scenes is a filtered listening illustration. The atmosphere model is hidden underground.

0.25 m below ground · Illustrative depth

Who shares dinner with a tree?

Fine roots meet fungal threads in the soil. In many of these partnerships, fungi bring water and nutrients; the plant shares sugars made in its leaves.

Rain above the soil, gently muffled. An illustrative listening scene, not a recording of roots.

Fact source
1 m below ground · Illustrative depth

Who dug these tiny tunnels?

Earthworms make passages through soil as they move and feed. These tunnels can become routes for air, water and plant roots. Different worms live at different depths.

Soft rain from the surface. The worm itself has no added sound effect.

Fact source
2 m below ground · Illustrative depth

Could you wait years for one summer?

Periodical cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground as nymphs, feeding on tree-root fluids. Their famous chorus comes later, when the males become adults above ground.

An adult cicada recording previews life above ground; it is not a sound made by the buried nymph.

Fact source
25 m below ground · Illustrative depth

Is that a train beneath your feet?

London opened the world’s first underground railway in 1863. Today, electric trains turn tunnels into busy streets beneath the city. Listen to a real Tube train arriving.

A London Underground train arriving and opening its doors. This depth illustrates a tunnel, not that recording’s measured location.

Fact source
40 m below ground · Illustrative depth

Is groundwater one enormous lake?

Usually it fills tiny connected pores and cracks in soil and rock. An aquifer is more like a water-filled sponge than a vast hollow tank. Water can travel through those connected spaces.

A quiet scene. Slowly moving pore water has no added rushing-river sound.

Fact source
80 m below ground · Illustrative depth

Can a drop of water build a tower?

Mineral-rich water can leave a little calcite behind with each drip. Over time, stalactites grow down from ceilings and stalagmites rise from cave floors. Listen to real drips echoing in a cavern.

Real dripping water in Treak Cliff Cavern, England. Some nearby pops are drops hitting a collection-vat lid.

Fact source
150 m below ground · Illustrative depth

Why does a cave sound so much bigger?

Sound reflects from hard rock. Reflections arriving together make a lingering reverberation; a clearly separated reflection is an echo. The room becomes part of what you hear.

The same real cavern recording, with its original room reflections. No artificial echo is added.

Fact source
600 m below ground · Illustrative depth

Can rocks grow their own decorations?

Mineral-rich water can leave crystals behind in caves. Calcite and gypsum form some of these decorations. Their delicate shapes are mineral growth, not plants.

Cave-drip ambience illustrates the setting. Crystals themselves are quiet.

Fact source
2800 m below ground · Measured depth

Can life get by without sunlight?

Researchers found a bacterial community in water 2.8 km down in a South African gold mine. Its energy supply came from rock-driven chemistry, rather than sunlight at the surface.

Quiet. No invented voice for microscopic life.

Fact source
12262 m below ground · Measured depth

How far have we drilled straight down?

The Kola Superdeep Borehole reached 12,262 m. Even there, the drill was still in Earth’s crust. It reached only about a third of the way through the crust at that location.

Quiet. There is no authenticated recording here from the bottom of this borehole.

Fact source

Ocean listening

The twilight, marine-snow and midnight scenes use a NOAA blue whale recording from the northeast Pacific at original speed, as ocean ambience rather than an exact-depth recording. CC0; excerpt converted to mono MP3, normalized, with edge fades.

Recording source and license

Ocean depths and Earth’s interior

A composite tour of different locations and depth datums. Ocean and interior artwork consists of distinct generated watercolor illustrations. Interior scenes are conceptual illustrations, not photographs or scale diagrams. Quiet exhibits contain no purported recordings from these depths.

Where does daylight start to fade?

200 m below sea level. Approximate zone boundary.

Below about 200 m, the ocean enters its twilight zone. There is still a little sunlight, but not enough for photosynthesis. This is a depth tour of different places, not one shaft beneath the city.

Real NOAA blue whale recording as ocean ambience; not captured at the displayed depth.

Scientific source

It snows down here. But it is not ice.

500 m below sea level. Illustrative depth.

Marine snow is a slow shower of organic debris from above. In the deep ocean, those sinking scraps help feed animals far from the sun.

Real NOAA blue whale recording as ocean ambience; not captured at the displayed depth.

Scientific source

What happens when the sun disappears?

1,000 m below sea level. Approximate zone boundary.

The midnight zone begins around 1,000 m. Sunlight no longer reaches these waters. A submarine needs its own lights to reveal the world outside.

Real NOAA blue whale recording as ocean ambience; not captured at the displayed depth.

Scientific source

Can a food chain run without sunshine?

2,500 m below sea level. Illustrative depth.

Around hydrothermal vents, microbes use chemical energy to make food. Hot water emerges through the seafloor, supporting communities in the darkness. Vent depths vary.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

A ship, resting in the dark.

3,800 m below sea level. Approximate wreck depth.

The wreck of Titanic lies about 3,800 m beneath the North Atlantic. Discovered in 1985, it is a maritime memorial as well as a window into history.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

Welcome to the abyss.

4,000 m below sea level. Approximate zone boundary.

At around 4,000 m, the abyssal zone begins. Much of the deep seafloor lies in this cold, dark realm. The deepest trenches still lie below.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

There is a world below the abyss.

6,000 m below sea level. Approximate zone boundary.

Below roughly 6,000 m lies the hadal zone, named after Hades. Its trenches are narrow, deep features rather than a continuous layer covering the whole ocean floor.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

A little fish with an enormous record.

8,336 m below sea level. Recorded observation.

In 2022, cameras filmed a snailfish 8,336 m down in the Izu-Ogasawara Trench near Japan. Its pale, delicate body belongs in a place that would crush ordinary equipment.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

The deepest known ocean floor.

10,935 m below sea level. Approximate measured depth.

Challenger Deep, in the Mariana Trench, reaches approximately 10,935 m below sea level. Put Mount Everest here and its summit would still be more than two kilometres underwater.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

We have left the drill behind.

35,000 m below Earth’s surface. Illustrative crust boundary.

No borehole reaches this far. Beneath continents, the crust is commonly tens of kilometres thick. Its lower boundary varies greatly; this 35 km stop is an illustration, not a worldwide floor.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

Solid rock that can slowly flow.

150,000 m below Earth’s surface. Illustrative mantle depth.

The mantle is mostly solid, not a giant ocean of magma. Over immense spans of time, hot rock can deform and flow. Here our journey follows scientific evidence rather than a tunnel.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

How do we see through a planet?

1,000,000 m below Earth’s surface. Illustrative mantle depth.

Earthquake waves travel differently through different materials. Their paths and arrival times let scientists investigate layers that no person or drill has ever reached.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

Here, the metal becomes liquid.

2,900,000 m below Earth’s surface. Approximate layer boundary.

About 2,900 km down, the rocky mantle gives way to the outer core. This layer is liquid metal, mostly iron. It is very different from the solid rock above.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

A solid heart inside liquid metal.

5,150,000 m below Earth’s surface. Approximate layer boundary.

Around 5,150 km down, we reach the inner core. Despite the immense heat, enormous pressure keeps this iron-rich inner region solid.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

Every direction leads back up.

6,371,000 m below Earth’s surface. Approximate mean Earth radius.

We have reached the centre in our imagined journey: about 6,371 km beneath the mean surface. The ocean trenches and deepest boreholes occupy only a tiny fraction of that distance.

Quiet exhibit. No recording from this depth is available in this journey.

Scientific source

What you hear above ground

34 stops play real recordings or related habitat ambience; 32 stay quiet. All clips are bundled locally. The table below identifies the actual species, recording location and any illustrative use. No clip claims to reproduce the exact sound level at a labelled altitude.

The bat call is slowed tenfold so its ultrasound is audible. The giraffe hum comes from the published study. The church uses its own recorded bell; the turbine recording identifies a 99.5 m hub height. Sliding the piano’s glass still muffles the music. Natural quiet replaces unsupported sound effects and unrelated species. Crossfades and volume changes are editorial, not calibrated decibel or hearing-range measurements.

Numbered route changes · Height evidence for the above-ground stops

Sources for the 66 above-ground stops

1 · 0 m · GROUND SURFACE

What is alive under your shoes?

Right at ground level, a teaspoon of good soil can hold up to a billion bacteria—tiny living things too small to see.

Fact source
2 · 0.18 m · REPORTED VERTICAL JUMP

How high can a flea jump?

A flea can jump about 18 cm straight up. Springy parts inside its body store energy, then release it in one tiny leap.

Fact source · Supporting source
3 · 0.33 m · EXPERIMENTAL VERTICAL SEPARATION

Can lifting a clock change its ticking?

Scientists lifted a super-precise clock just 33 cm. It ticked a tiny bit faster because Earth’s pull was slightly weaker.

Fact source
4 · 0.5 m · UPPER REPORTED PLANT HEIGHT

Where does this tiny parachute take off?

Dandelions can grow 50 cm tall. When the wind catches their fluffy seeds, each seed floats away like a little parachute.

Fact source · Supporting source
5 · 1.21 m · INSTRUMENT HEIGHT

How does a piano this tall make music?

A Yamaha U1 piano stands 1.21 m tall. Press a key and a little hammer hits strings inside to make a note.

Fact source · Supporting source
6 · 2 m · CALCULATED VIEW FROM EYES 2 m ABOVE SEA LEVEL

How far can you see when you stand by the sea?

If your eyes are 2 m above a flat sea, the horizon is about 5 km away. Climb higher and you can see farther.

Fact source
7 · 2.72 m · MEASURED STANDING HEIGHT

How tall was the tallest person?

Robert Wadlow grew to 2.72 m tall—taller than most doorways. He was measured in 1940 and remains the tallest person ever reliably recorded.

Fact source
8 · 3 m · RECOMMENDED MINIMUM NEST-BOX HEIGHT

How high should a barn owl’s home be?

A barn owl nest box should be at least 3 m above the ground. From its high home, the owl can fly out to hunt.

Fact source
9 · 3.2 m · AVERAGE MALE SHOULDER-HEIGHT RANGE

How tall is an elephant’s shoulder?

Male African savanna elephants average about 3–3.2 m at the shoulder. These huge animals make deep rumbles to talk to each other.

Fact source · Supporting source
10 · 5 m · EXPERIMENTAL NEST-BOX HEIGHT

Would bees choose an upstairs home?

In nest-choice tests, honeybees preferred a home 5 m above the ground over one just 1 m up. A hollow tree can become their buzzing home.

Fact source
11 · 5.5 m · MAXIMUM REPORTED MALE HEIGHT

What sound comes from this tall animal?

Male giraffes can reach 5.5 m tall. Scientists recorded giraffes making soft, low hums at night.

Fact source · Supporting source
12 · 8 m · WITHIN OBSERVED NEST HEIGHTS · 3–12 m ABOVE GROUND

Where does a hummingbird hide its nest?

Ruby-throated hummingbirds usually build nests about 3–12 m above the ground. Each little nest is only about as wide as a golf ball.

Fact source
13 · 9 m · REPORTED FORAGING HEIGHT · BELOW ABOUT 9 m

Who hunts with sound above your head?

Big brown bats often hunt below about 9 m at Mount Rainier. They call and listen for echoes to find insects; this recording is slowed so we can hear it.

Fact source
14 · 10 m · STANDARD WIND-MEASUREMENT HEIGHT

Why measure the wind this high?

Weather stations usually measure wind 10 m above the ground. Up here, nearby grass and small obstacles have less effect on the reading.

Fact source
15 · 10.9 m · MEASURED PLANT RECORD · 2025

Can a sunflower grow taller than a house?

Alex Babich grew a sunflower 10.90 m tall in 2025. That is about the height of a three-storey house!

Fact source
16 · 27 m · COMPETITION PLATFORM ABOVE WATER

Would you jump from this high?

Men’s championship high divers leap from a platform 27 m above the water. They turn in the air and enter the water feet first.

Fact source
17 · 30 m · APPROXIMATE BUILDING HEIGHT

Can mud bricks make a tall tower?

In Shibam, Yemen, people built mud-brick homes around 30 m tall. Thick walls at the bottom help support the rooms stacked above.

Fact source · Supporting source
18 · 40 m · OCCASIONAL MAXIMUM ERUPTION HEIGHT ABOVE VENT

Can hot water shoot this high?

Iceland’s Strokkur geyser can sometimes throw hot water 40 m into the air. Water heated underground bursts upward in a sudden spray.

Fact source · Supporting source
19 · 48.8 m · UPPER REPORTED NEST HEIGHT · 160 ft

Who builds a nest almost 50 m up?

Black-crowned night herons can nest up to about 49 m above the ground. These birds often hunt after dark and make rough, croaking calls.

Fact source
20 · 60 m · TOWER HEIGHT ABOVE GROUND

Where is this ringing coming from?

Berlin’s Samariter Church has a 60 m tower. Listen to its real bells ringing out over the neighbourhood.

Fact source
21 · 67 m · HIGHEST ROOF ABOVE SEA LEVEL

How high do these stone sails reach?

The tallest roof of the Sydney Opera House reaches 67 m above sea level. Inside, people fill its halls with music and theatre.

Fact source
22 · 80 m · WITHIN REPORTED NEST-CLIFF HEIGHTS · 8–400 m

Could a falcon make its home up here?

Peregrine falcons nest on cliffs from about 8 to 400 m high, sometimes higher. A ledge at this height gives them a lookout over the ground.

Fact source
23 · 83.8 m · MEASURED TREE HEIGHT ABOVE BASE

Is the biggest tree also the tallest?

The General Sherman tree is 83.8 m tall. Its huge, thick trunk makes it the world’s largest living tree by wood volume.

Fact source
24 · 99.5 m · RECORDED TURBINE HUB HEIGHT · SIEMENS SWT-2.3-101

What is turning almost 100 m up?

The centre of this wind turbine’s blades is 99.5 m above the ground. Wind turns the blades to make electricity; you can hear a real recording of this turbine model.

Fact source
25 · 116 m · APPROXIMATE MAXIMUM TREE HEIGHT

How can a tree drink this high up?

The tallest coast redwoods reach about 116 m above their roots. Water leaving their leaves helps pull more water all the way up the trunk.

Fact source · Supporting source
26 · 146.5 m · ORIGINAL BUILDING HEIGHT ABOVE BASE

How high did the Great Pyramid once reach?

Egypt’s Great Pyramid originally stood 146.5 m tall. Built over 4,000 years ago, it was the world’s tallest building for thousands of years.

Fact source
27 · 183 m · DUNE HEIGHT ABOVE BASE

Can a hill of sand make a sound?

California’s Kelso Dunes rise about 183 m above their base. When dry sand slides down their sides, the dunes can make a deep booming sound.

Fact source
28 · 200 m · WITHIN TYPICAL CLOUD-BASE RANGE · 0–370 m ABOVE GROUND

Can a cloud hang just above the rooftops?

Low, flat stratus clouds can start anywhere from ground level to about 370 m up. If one touches the ground, you walk through it as fog.

Fact source
29 · 330 m · STRUCTURE HEIGHT ABOVE GROUND

Can sunshine make a tower lean?

The Eiffel Tower reaches 330 m above the ground. Sunshine warms one side more than the other, making its top move a little.

Fact source
30 · 343 m · MAXIMUM STRUCTURAL HEIGHT ABOVE GROUND

Can a bridge reach higher than the Eiffel Tower?

The tallest part of France’s Millau Viaduct reaches 343 m above the ground. Its roadway carries cars across a deep river valley.

Fact source
31 · 400 m · WITHIN MEASURED MIGRATION LAYER · 150–1,200 m ABOVE GROUND

Is there a river of insects over our heads?

Radar spotted insects travelling 150–1,200 m above southern England. Researchers estimated that 3.5 trillion passed overhead in a year.

Fact source
32 · 508 m · STRUCTURE HEIGHT ABOVE GROUND

How does this tall tower stay steady?

Taipei 101 stands 508 m tall. A giant heavy ball hanging inside moves against the building’s sway, helping it rock less in the wind.

Fact source
33 · 524 m · MEASURED WAVE RUN-UP ABOVE SEA LEVEL

How far up a mountain can a wave climb?

In Alaska’s Lituya Bay in 1958, a landslide made a wave rush 524 m up a hillside. It stripped trees from the slope.

Fact source
34 · 610 m · WITHIN TYPICAL CLOUD-BASE RANGE · 2,000–10,000 ft

Where can a long rainy day begin?

Thick nimbostratus clouds often have bases about 600–3,000 m above the ground. They spread across the sky and bring long spells of rain or snow.

Fact source
35 · 828 m · STRUCTURE HEIGHT ABOVE GROUND

How far above the street does this tower reach?

Dubai’s Burj Khalifa rises 828 m above the ground. Its narrow top is more than twice as high as the Eiffel Tower.

Fact source
36 · 979 m · TOTAL WATERFALL DROP

How long is the world’s tallest waterfall?

Angel Falls in Venezuela drops 979 m from top to bottom. Wind can turn some of its falling water into a cloud of mist.

Fact source
37 · 1000 m · CALCULATED SOUND DELAY FOR A 1 km VERTICAL PATH

If lightning flashes 1 km overhead, when will you hear it?

About 3 seconds later. Light reaches you almost at once, but the thunder takes time to travel down through the air.

Fact source
38 · 1086 m · APPROXIMATE SUMMIT ELEVATION ABOVE SEA LEVEL

Why does this mountain wear a tablecloth?

Table Mountain reaches about 1,086 m above the sea. Damp air blowing up its slopes can cool into a white cloud that spills over the top.

Fact source · Supporting source
39 · 2240 m · CITY ELEVATION ABOVE SEA LEVEL

What happened at this high-up Olympic stadium?

Mexico City sits about 2,240 m above the sea. There, Bob Beamon jumped 8.90 m forward across the sand in 1968—a world record that lasted nearly 23 years.

Fact source · Supporting source
40 · 2500 m · OBSERVED TWILIGHT ASCENT · ABOVE GROUND

Who flies this high as the sun goes down?

Common swifts can climb about 2,500 m above the ground at dawn and dusk. These small birds can even spend the night flying.

Fact source
41 · 3000 m · ALTITUDE-DEPENDENT UV RULE OF THUMB

Why is mountain sunshine stronger?

At 3,000 m above the sea, there is less air overhead to block the Sun’s burning rays. UV levels rise roughly 10% for every 1,000 m you climb.

Fact source
42 · 3571 m · VIEWING-TERRACE ELEVATION ABOVE SEA LEVEL

Can you ride a lift into a mountaintop?

The Sphinx viewing terrace in Switzerland sits 3,571 m above the sea. A lift inside the mountain carries visitors up to its snowy lookout.

Fact source
43 · 3812 m · APPROXIMATE LAKE-SURFACE ELEVATION

Can boats sail higher than many mountains?

Lake Titicaca’s water lies about 3,812 m above the sea. People sail boats across this huge lake high in the Andes.

Fact source
44 · 4000 m · WITHIN OBSERVED SAHARAN AIR LAYER

Can desert dust fly across an ocean?

Saharan dust often travels in a layer about 1,500–6,000 m above the sea. Winds can carry it all the way across the Atlantic Ocean.

Fact source
45 · 4500 m · REPORTED AERIAL CAPTURE ALTITUDE ABOVE SEA LEVEL

Can a spider fly higher than a mountain?

Spiders have been found about 4,500 m above the sea. They let out silk threads and ride the moving air like tiny balloon travellers.

Fact source
46 · 5000 m · OBSERVATORY ELEVATION ABOVE SEA LEVEL

Why put these giant dishes on a high desert?

The ALMA telescopes stand 5,000 m above the sea in Chile. The thin, dry air lets faint light from space reach their giant dishes.

Fact source
47 · 5500 m · APPROXIMATE HALF-PRESSURE LEVEL · STANDARD ATMOSPHERE

Have we already climbed past half the air?

At about 5,500 m above the sea, air pressure is roughly half its sea-level value. About half the atmosphere’s weight is already below you.

Fact source
48 · 6263 m · SUMMIT ELEVATION ABOVE SEA LEVEL

Which mountaintop is farthest from Earth’s middle?

Chimborazo rises 6,263 m above the sea. Earth bulges around its middle, giving this Ecuadorian summit a head start that puts it farther from Earth’s centre than Everest.

Fact source
49 · 6739 m · LIVE-CAPTURE ELEVATION ABOVE SEA LEVEL

Can a mouse live this high?

Scientists caught a live leaf-eared mouse on a volcano 6,739 m above the sea. This tiny mammal was living where the air is thin and the ground is freezing.

Fact source
50 · 8000 m · APPROXIMATE HIGH-ALTITUDE PHYSIOLOGICAL ZONE

Why is it so hard to breathe up here?

Above about 8,000 m, each breath brings in very little oxygen. Climbers call this the death zone because the human body cannot stay healthy here for long.

Fact source
51 · 8500 m · WITHIN AIRCRAFT SAMPLING RANGE · 8–15 km ABOVE SEA LEVEL

Are tiny living things floating this high?

Scientists flying about 8,000–15,000 m above the sea found bacteria in the air. These tiny living passengers had travelled far above the ground.

Fact source
52 · 8849 m · SUMMIT LANDING · CURRENT ROUNDED SUMMIT ELEVATION

Could a helicopter land on the top of Everest?

In 2005, Didier Delsalle landed a helicopter on Everest’s summit, about 8,849 m above the sea. Its spinning blades lifted it through the thin mountain air.

Fact source
53 · 11000 m · STANDARD-ATMOSPHERE CALCULATION ABOVE SEA LEVEL

Does sound travel more slowly up here?

In the cold air about 11,000 m up, sound travels roughly 295 m each second. Near sea level on a mild day, it travels about 340 m each second.

Fact source
54 · 18000 m · APPROXIMATE CRUISING ALTITUDE ABOVE SEA LEVEL

Could a passenger plane fly this high?

Concorde carried passengers about 18,000 m above the sea. It flew faster than sound, and the hot air rubbing past made its body grow a little longer.

Fact source
55 · 19000 m · APPROXIMATE BODY-TEMPERATURE BOILING THRESHOLD

Can warm water boil without getting hotter?

At about 19,000 m, the air pushes so weakly that exposed water can boil at body temperature. A person needs a sealed, pressurised suit to survive.

Fact source
56 · 21027 m · HOT-AIR BALLOON RECORD · ABOVE SEA LEVEL

How high has a hot-air balloon flown?

Vijaypat Singhania reached 21,027 m above the sea in a hot-air balloon in 2005. A burner heated the air inside the balloon to help it rise.

Fact source
57 · 25000 m · WITHIN THE OZONE-RICH STRATOSPHERE

What protects us from the Sun up here?

Much of Earth’s ozone lies about 15–35 km above the ground. This gas soaks up harmful rays from the Sun, helping protect life below.

Fact source
58 · 35000 m · APPROXIMATE STANDARD-ATMOSPHERE PRESSURE COMPARISON

Is the air here as thin as the air on Mars?

Around 35,000 m above Earth, air pressure is roughly like it is at the surface of Mars. This real Mars recording lets you hear a helicopter in that thin air.

Fact source
59 · 41422 m · PARACHUTE EXIT ALTITUDE ABOVE SEA LEVEL · 2014

How high did Alan Eustace jump from?

In 2014, Alan Eustace rose by balloon to 41,422 m above the sea. Wearing a special pressure suit, he let go and parachuted back to Earth.

Fact source
60 · 53700 m · RESEARCH BALLOON ALTITUDE ABOVE SEA LEVEL · 2013

Can a balloon climb higher than a jet?

A Japanese research balloon reached 53,700 m above the sea in 2013. Its skin was much thinner than a sheet of paper.

Fact source
61 · 57000 m · MEASURED PLUME-TOP ELEVATION ABOVE SEA LEVEL

How high can a volcano throw its cloud?

Tonga’s huge eruption in 2022 sent a plume about 57,000 m above the sea. Scientists measured it using pictures from weather satellites.

Fact source
62 · 70000 m · WITHIN TYPICAL METEOR-GLOW ALTITUDES · 50–80 km

Why do shooting stars glow?

Most meteors glow about 50–80 km above the ground. Bits of space rock rush into the air so fast that the rock and nearby air heat up and shine.

Fact source
63 · 80467 m · US 50-MILE RECOGNITION THRESHOLD

Have we reached space yet?

At about 80,467 m, you have climbed 50 miles. The United States uses that height to recognise space travellers; another widely used space boundary is 100 km.

Fact source
64 · 85000 m · APPROXIMATE POLAR MESOSPHERIC CLOUD ALTITUDE

Can a cloud glow after sunset?

Tiny ice clouds form around 85,000 m above the ground. They can still catch sunlight after the land below has gone dark.

Fact source
65 · 90000 m · APPROXIMATE SODIUM-LAYER ALTITUDE

How can a telescope make a star?

About 90,000 m up, there is a thin layer of sodium atoms. A telescope’s laser makes them glow, creating a guide star that helps sharpen its view.

Fact source
66 · 100000 m · GRAVITY CALCULATED 100 km ABOVE EARTH

Has gravity disappeared?

Even 100 km up, Earth’s pull is about 97% as strong as at the ground. Astronauts float in orbit because they and their spacecraft are falling around Earth together.

Fact source

Artwork & loading

Retained watercolor illustrations are joined by new interpretive watercolor cutouts generated with the built-in image generator. Images are not measured scientific diagrams or reconstructions of historical photographs. They use the original subtle motion and touch effects.

Nearby illustrations load first and remain mounted for revisits. Current-scene recordings are prefetched and decoded when needed; fonts and audio are bundled locally. No external image or audio host is required during the journey.
